source: Invest Like the Best — Why the markets are pricing AI wrong: July 2026 AI/semis selloff, private inference cloud, old-GPU repricing, ~$700B Blackwell/Rubin credit gap
summary: Claude/LLM homogenization of investment analysis is creating artificial volatility cycles and breakdown of market diversity
summary_extended: Baker argues that the widespread adoption of LLMs — specifically Claude — as the primary analytical tool for public equity investors (both retail and institutional) is creating a dangerous homogenization of market interpretation, which he dubs the 'Walter Cronkite effect.' Because nearly all investors are feeding the same news into the same AI model and receiving probabilistically similar outputs, the diversity of analytical opinion that normally stabilizes markets is collapsing, a structural risk consistent with Mauboussin's theory on the importance of analytical diversity for efficient price discovery. Baker cites Japanese capacitor stocks as a concrete example: an entire multi-year fundamental cycle was compressed into six weeks driven purely by AI-generated narrative, before any underlying fundamentals had actually materialized. The investment implication is that this homogenization creates exploitable mispricings — situations where AI-driven consensus overshoots or undershoots reality — and that investors who can identify where the AI narrative diverges from fundamentals have a structural edge. Baker frames this as a near-term and ongoing structural market risk rather than a one-time event.
detail: Most public equity investors (retail and institutional) are now feeding every piece of news into Claude, which interprets it probabilistically with little variation across users. This is creating a 'Walter Cronkite effect' — everyone trading on the same AI interpretation. Evidence: Japanese capacitor stocks completed an entire multi-year cycle in 6 weeks based on narrative, before fundamentals even hit. This breakdown of analytical diversity (per Mauboussin's theory) is a structural market risk creating exploitable mispricings.
confidence_evidence: Baker presents this as an observed phenomenon with a specific example (Japanese capacitor stocks) but it's a qualitative/structural observation
